projects.label_rationale: Two separate endpoints (create and update) both missing @Valid on the same DTO type, with authorization otherwise correctly applied at the class level - i.e. CWE-20 twice, nothing else. Labelled before scanning, and deliberately: a rule that only looks at 'the single highest-severity finding present' would score this project identically to unvalidated-orders-service (one CWE-20 finding, medium) because CWE-20's own base score never changes. This project is labelled high instead, on the judgment that the *same* validation gap recurring across multiple endpoints signals a systemic pattern in how this codebase was generated, not an isolated slip - and a systemic weakness is worse than a one-off. This is the intended divergence case against a naive max-severity baseline: exists specifically so Chapter 5 can show whether Layer 4 (which has a finding_count/medium_count feature that can see the repetition) predicts this correctly where a single-max-score baseline structurally cannot.

projects.label: critical
projects.label_rationale: Codex-generated, post-hoc label. No security dependency of any kind is declared (spring-security-crypto is used only for BCrypt hashing, not access control) - zero centralized or annotation-based authorization exists anywhere. Of the four CWE-284 findings, signup/login are expected to be reachable without prior authentication (that is how login works); get and update are the real problem - either accepts any numeric id with no check that the caller is that user, so any caller can read or overwrite any other user's profile: a functional unauthenticated account-takeover path on a service whose entire purpose is account data. Labelled critical on the severity of that specific gap, not the raw finding count - password handling itself (BCryptPasswordEncoder, .matches() not ==) is done correctly and contributes nothing to this label.

projects.label: medium
projects.label_rationale: Codex-generated, post-hoc label. All three CWE-284 findings fire because this project protects its endpoints with a hand-rolled X-Admin-Key header check against an environment-provided value, not any Spring annotation or SecurityFilterChain this tool's CWE-284 rule recognizes - a third real-world variant of the annotation-blindness limitation documented in IMPLEMENTATION_LOG.md's 2026-09-03 entry. This is not wide open: every sensitive method is gated behind an authorized(key) check before it runs. Labelled medium, not low, because the mechanism itself is weaker than idiomatic per-user authorization - one shared static key rather than per-user identity, and a plain .equals() comparison on that key rather than a constant-time comparison - so it earns real credit for having a gate at all without being treated as equivalent to properly-scoped auth.

projects.label: low
projects.label_rationale: Codex-generated, post-hoc label, batch 2 (no security mention in the prompt). Neither endpoint has a login-based gate, but unlike every other unprotected project in this dataset, that is the correct design here: a password-reset flow must be reachable by a user who is, by definition, not currently able to log in. The real security-relevant work is done well - a 32-byte SecureRandom token, the token hashed (SHA-256) before being stored so the in-memory map never holds the raw value, a 15-minute expiry, and the confirm step requiring possession of that single-use token as its own authentication factor. A second, distinct kind of true-positive-but-inconsequential case for this dataset (after ai-product-catalog-service's 'genuinely public data' case): here the endpoint being reachable without prior auth is not an oversight but a domain necessity, and the actual security controls that do matter for this flow are implemented correctly.
